transcript.text: Samsung microwave runs, light on, plate turns, fan going, but the food comes out stone cold. Watched a YouTube video on testing the magnetron - I've got the cover screws out already, what should I check first?

## Before you touch anything inside: discharge the capacitor

The high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even after the microwave is unplugged, sometimes for days. It's in the circuit with the transformer and magnetron, and it's what kills people doing this repair. Do this first, every time you've had it plugged in:

1. Unplug it. Don't rely on the switch.
2. Find the HV capacitor, a metal cylinder or oval can, usually near the transformer.
3. Using a screwdriver with a well-insulated handle (or a proper discharge tool / 10kΩ+ resistor with insulated leads), touch the metal shaft to the chassis, then bridge across both capacitor terminals, and then each terminal to the chassis. Keep one hand away from the unit.
4. Expect a possible snap/spark. Do it twice to be sure.

Never test anything with the microwave plugged in and the cover off. All checks below are done unplugged with a multimeter.

## Quick check before going further: demo mode

Some Samsung models have a demo/showroom mode where everything runs (light, turntable, fan) but nothing heats. That matches your symptoms exactly. Look for "dEMO" or a "D" on the display, and check your manual for how to toggle it (often holding Stop/Cancel or a number key for a few seconds). Worth ruling out before replacing parts.

## Testing order (most likely culprits first)

1. High-voltage diode (often fails, cheap)
• Usually connected between the capacitor and chassis.
• Most multimeters can't fully test it, but if it reads near zero ohms in both directions (shorted) or shows open in both directions with a 9V battery in series, it's bad.
• Many people just replace it along with the capacitor since they're inexpensive.

2. High-voltage capacitor
• Look for bulging, leaking oil, or burn marks.
• Terminal to metal case should read open (infinite). Any continuity means it's bad.
• If your meter has capacitance mode, it should be close to the µF rating printed on it.

3. Magnetron
• Disconnect its wires (photograph them first).
• Between the two filament terminals: should be under ~1 ohm. Open = dead.
• Each terminal to the metal case: should be open (infinite). Any reading means it's shorted.
• Also check the thermal cutoff/fuse often mounted on the magnetron. It should show continuity.

4. HV fuse (some models have one inline): should show continuity.

5. High-voltage transformer (less common failure)
• Primary winding: roughly 1-2 ohms
• Secondary (HV) winding: roughly 50-150 ohms
• Filament winding: near 0 ohms

Exact values vary by model. If you post your model number (sticker inside the door frame or on the back), I can help narrow down which parts it has and typical specs.

## A few more notes

• If your model is an inverter type (an inverter board instead of a big heavy transformer), the testing is different and the board itself is a common failure point. Let me know if you see that.
• Take photos of all wiring before disconnecting anything.
• If parts plus your time approach the cost of a new microwave, replacement is often the more sensible call. Magnetrons especially can be pricey.

What do you see in there: a big transformer, or a circuit board where the transformer would be?

Haven't discharged anything, don't really know what the capacitor is or which bit is which in there. It's unplugged though. Display is normal countdown, no dEMO. Model is MS23K3513AW/EU. No insulated discharge tool either, just my screwdrivers.

## Stop and don't touch anything inside yet

Unplugged doesn't mean safe. The high-voltage capacitor stores charge independently of the mains. It's designed to drain itself through a built-in resistor, but if that resistor has failed (and you're already dealing with a fault in the high-voltage section), it can hold a charge that can kill you. Until it's discharged, keep your hands, tools, and meter probes out.

Since you can't yet identify the parts and don't have a proper tool, you're at the riskiest point of this repair. There's no shame in screwing the cover back on here.

## Is it worth fixing?

The MS23K3513AW is an inexpensive model (roughly £90-120 new). A magnetron alone is often £30-60, and you may not know which part has failed until you've tested several. A repair shop will likely cost more than a new microwave. If you'd rather not risk it, replacing it is a perfectly sensible call. Take the old one to a recycling centre (WEEE) rather than the bin.

## If you do want to carry on

Identify the parts by looking only, without touching:
• Transformer: the heaviest thing in there, a big block of stacked metal plates with copper windings, bolted to the base.
• Capacitor: a metal can (cylinder or flattened oval, roughly the size of a fat deodorant can) with two spade terminals on top. Its label shows a rating in µF and something like "2100VAC". It's wired to the transformer.
• Diode: a small black cylinder with a wire running from the capacitor to a screw on the chassis.
• Magnetron: a squarish metal unit with cooling fins, mounted on the side of the cooking chamber, with two wires on spade terminals.

Discharging with an ordinary screwdriver (one with a plastic handle, no cracks):
1. Leave it unplugged.
2. Hold the screwdriver only by the handle, and keep your other hand out of the microwave (in your pocket helps).
3. Rest the metal shaft against the bare metal chassis, then slide it over so it bridges both capacitor terminals at once. A snap or spark is normal.
4. Then touch each terminal individually to the chassis.
5. Repeat the whole thing a second time.

If anything about that feels uncertain, don't do it.

## Likely culprits for your symptoms

Everything runs but nothing heats on a model like this, so the usual suspects are:
1. HV diode, which fails often and is cheap
2. HV capacitor
3. Magnetron, including the small thermal cutoff fitted on or near it
4. Transformer, which is less common
5. Relay on the control board that switches power to the transformer

Once it's discharged, photograph all the wiring before disconnecting anything. I can then talk you through testing each part with a multimeter. Do you have a multimeter, and does it have a capacitance or diode setting?
Yeah I've got a multimeter. Not sure if it has a capacitance or diode setting, I'd have to look. Is the screwdriver discharge OK to do with mine, it's got a plastic handle?

## Yes, a plastic-handled screwdriver is the standard way to do it, if it passes these checks

Check the screwdriver first:
• Handle intact: no cracks, chips, or splits.
• No metal running through the handle: some screwdrivers have a metal cap on the end or a shaft that goes all the way through ("strike-through" types). If you can see metal at the butt end, don't use it.
• Long enough shaft that your fingers stay well back from the terminals.
• Ideally VDE / 1000V rated (a red/yellow handle marked "1000V"). Not essential for discharging, but if you have one, use it. They're about £5-10 if you want to buy one.

Then discharge:
1. Unplugged. Hold the screwdriver only by the handle, and put your other hand in your pocket or behind your back.
2. Touch the metal shaft to bare chassis metal (an unpainted screw or bracket).
3. Keep it touching the chassis and slide it onto the capacitor terminal nearest the transformer, then the other terminal.
4. Bridge both capacitor terminals together with the shaft.
5. Repeat the whole thing a second time.

A snap or spark is normal and means it held a charge. Nothing happening is also fine, since the built-in bleeder resistor may already have drained it. A small burn mark on the screwdriver tip is just cosmetic.

Confirm it's safe: Only do this after discharging, because most meters aren't rated for the ~2000V a charged capacitor can hold. Set the meter to DC volts on its highest range and measure across the two capacitor terminals. It should read 0V or very close to it. If it shows anything significant, discharge again.

## Finding the settings on your multimeter

• Diode test: a symbol like an arrow pointing at a bar (▶|), often sharing a position with the continuity beep.
• Capacitance: marked F, µF, or a symbol like -||-.

If you don't have them, that's fine. The most useful first test, the magnetron, only needs the ohms (Ω) setting.

## Once it's discharged: magnetron test (ohms only)

1. Photograph the two wires on the magnetron terminals, then pull them off.
2. Across the two terminals: you should get a very low reading, under about 1Ω.
• Open or "OL" means the filament has failed and the magnetron is bad.
3. Each terminal to the magnetron's metal body: should read "OL" (open).
• Any reading means the magnetron is shorted and bad.

If the magnetron passes, the capacitor and diode are next. Tell me what your meter can do and what readings you get, and I'll walk you through them.

Rediscs the capacitor whenever it's been plugged back in for a test run, every time, before your hands go back inside.
